paragraphs: Robust learning asks whether a model can perform well under unfavorable changes in its data distribution. Some methods use stable relationships across training environments to provide guarantees. Those guarantees can depend on having sufficiently varied environments to determine the relevant worst-case risk. This paper studies what robustness can mean when the available training distributions identify that risk only partially.

The authors introduce identifiable robust risk and a corresponding population minimax quantity. Together, these describe the best robustness achievable given the information available, independently of any particular learning algorithm. This changes the benchmark for evaluating methods: the comparison accounts for uncertainty that the training environments cannot resolve. The paper develops these concepts broadly and then examines them in linear structural causal models.

Using this benchmark, the authors prove that previous approaches can deliver suboptimal robustness under partial identifiability. Simulations and real-world experiments support the analysis. Existing methods become increasingly suboptimal as more test variation occurs in directions absent during training. The contribution is a framework for separating what robustness is achievable from what current methods actually achieve.
neurips-2024-achievable-distributional-r.tldr: The paper defines achievable robustness when training environments reveal only part of the worst-case risk and shows why existing methods can fall short.

paragraphs: Virtual try-on systems generate images showing how garments would look on a person. Supporting several garments together adds a challenge: the model must incorporate their visual information while producing a coherent fit. AnyFit addresses this alongside problems with garment styling, training instability, and image quality across different scenarios.

Its central component is the Hydra Block, a lightweight operator designed to accommodate combinations of attire. Parallel attention lets multiple branches, each carrying garment information, contribute features to the main network. The method also combines residuals from multiple models to improve its behavior across settings. A separate mask region boost strategy addresses instability associated with information leakage in existing approaches.

The authors report that AnyFit exceeds all evaluated baselines by a large margin on high-resolution benchmarks and real-world data. They describe outputs with well-fitting garments, realistic appearance, and detailed textures. These findings support the combined design for handling multiple garments and varied imagery. The evidence concerns the evaluated settings; the title’s broad ambition is reflected in the system’s emphasis on flexible attire combinations and scenario coverage.
neurips-2024-anyfit-controllable-virtual.tldr: AnyFit combines parallel garment attention and training improvements to produce detailed virtual try-on images across varied outfits and scenarios.

paragraphs: Generating synthetic database records requires more than reproducing the contents of individual tables. Real databases can contain many linked tables, with meaningful correlations between attributes stored far apart. Earlier methods struggle both with scaling to larger collections and with retaining these relationships. ClavaDDPM targets this interconnected setting.

The method combines diffusion-based generation with cluster labels that act as intermediate representations of relationships between tables. It specifically accounts for foreign key constraints, which connect records across tables. Algorithms propagate the learned latent variables through these connections, allowing information about relationships to influence generation beyond a single table. The cluster representation therefore provides a way to coordinate the generation of related data.

Evaluations on multi-table datasets of different sizes show substantially better preservation of long-range dependencies than existing methods. At the same time, ClavaDDPM remains competitive on measures of single-table usefulness. These are distinct findings: the method improves cross-table relationships without giving up competitive performance within individual tables. Its main contribution is extending strong tabular generation capabilities to the relational structure that makes a database more than a collection of separate datasets.
neurips-2024-clavaddpm-multi-relational-.tldr: ClavaDDPM uses cluster-guided diffusion to generate linked tables while better preserving correlations across the database.

paragraphs: Negotiation tests whether language models can coordinate with others while pursuing an assigned objective. It brings cooperation, competition, and possible manipulation into the same interaction. This paper turns negotiation into a scorable evaluation setting, addressing the limited understanding of how models communicate and make decisions in multi-agent environments.

The authors construct games involving multiple participants, multiple issues, and rich descriptions of the negotiating situation. Reaching agreement requires combining arithmetic, inference, exploration, and planning over several exchanges. They introduce metrics for both performance and consistency with assigned roles. They also provide procedures for generating new games and increasing difficulty, allowing the benchmark to evolve rather than remain a fixed collection of scenarios.

The evaluation examines interactions involving greedy and adversarial players as a safety concern. GPT-3.5 and smaller models mostly fail on the benchmark, while GPT-4 and leading large models, including Llama-3 70b, still struggle to reach agreement in harder and non-cooperative games. These results identify negotiation as a demanding test of coordinated reasoning and role-following, beyond producing plausible conversational responses.
neurips-2024-cooperation-competition-and.tldr: A scorable negotiation benchmark exposes substantial weaknesses in language models’ ability to reach agreements under competition and adversarial influence.

paragraphs: Many language models need similar behavioral adjustments, such as following instructions or avoiding sensitive information. Training each model separately repeats work, especially when models differ in size and vocabulary. Cross-model Control investigates whether a small trained component can carry an adjustment from one language model to others.

The approach starts from an observed similarity: fine-tuning produces remarkably similar shifts in output logits across different models. Logits are the scores that determine which tokens a model is likely to generate. The authors train a tiny language model alongside a frozen template model so that the small model learns to modify these scores. This component is intended to remain portable after that single training process.

Different vocabularies complicate applying the same controller to multiple models. The paper introduces PM-MinED, a token mapping strategy that supports this transfer. Experiments on instruction tuning and unlearning demonstrate the effectiveness of the overall method. The contribution is a way to reuse learned output adjustments across models, connecting an empirical similarity in fine-tuning behavior to a practical mechanism for reducing repeated training.
neurips-2024-cross-model-control-improvi.tldr: Cross-model Control trains a tiny portable model to adjust multiple language models’ outputs, including across different vocabularies.

paragraphs: A model can be adjusted for group fairness using validation data that includes sensitive attributes. Meta-learning provides a framework for choosing these adjustments, but different subgroups can favor conflicting update directions. The paper identifies these hypergradient conflicts as a source of unstable optimization and damage to both predictive performance and fairness.

The authors treat the conflicting groups as participants in a cooperative bargaining game. Their first training stage uses a Nash Bargaining Solution to combine the update directions and move toward the Pareto front, where further improvement involves tradeoffs among objectives. A second stage then optimizes the particular fairness objective of interest. This separates resolving competing directions from pursuing a chosen fairness criterion.

The theoretical results include a derivation of the bargaining solution for gradient aggregation without requiring linear independence, along with proofs of Pareto improvement and monotonic improvement in validation loss. Experiments examine several fairness objectives across six fairness datasets and two image classification tasks. The approach offers a principled way to manage subgroup conflicts inside the optimization process, rather than simply inserting fairness goals into meta-learning.
neurips-2024-fairness-aware-meta-learnin.tldr: The method uses Nash bargaining to reconcile conflicting subgroup updates before optimizing a specific fairness objective.

paragraphs: In offline model-based optimization, the goal is to find a high-scoring design using an existing dataset, without repeatedly evaluating the true objective. This matters when evaluations are constrained by time or safety. The paper develops a method that learns sequences of improving designs, building on the idea that an optimization trajectory can be a useful object to generate.

First, the authors construct synthetic trajectories from the available data. They introduce a preference for local relationships so that the trajectories have consistent improvement directions. A conditional diffusion model then learns to generate these sequences based on their scores. During generation, guidance steers multiple sampled trajectories toward high-scoring regions beyond those represented in the dataset.

A proxy function evaluates generated candidates and helps select promising designs from the trajectories. Thus, the method connects trajectory construction, score-conditioned generation, and candidate selection in one workflow. Experiments report better results than competitive baselines on Design-Bench and practical variants. The stated finding supports generating guided improvement paths as an effective approach to offline optimization, where access to new evaluations of the real function is restricted.
neurips-2024-guided-trajectory-generatio.tldr: The method trains a guided diffusion model on synthetic improvement trajectories to propose high-scoring designs from offline data.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit learners choose actions from contextual information and observe rewards. This paper studies how low reward variance can reduce regret, the accumulated loss relative to optimal choices. It assumes realizability: the function class can represent the true expected rewards. The analysis shows that eluder dimension, a measure of function-class complexity, matters crucially for variance-sensitive guarantees.

The authors distinguish adversaries that choose variance before seeing the action from those that choose it afterward. For the weaker adversary, the lower bound involves total variance and the smaller of action count and eluder dimension, under a stated dimension condition. A nearly matching upper bound applies when action count does not exceed that dimension and variance is revealed before each round. For the stronger adversary, the paper establishes lower and upper bounds with different dependence on dimension.

The authors also examine access to reward-distribution information. They show an existing bound cannot be improved in the stated regime. With Gaussian rewards and a modified definition of total variance, a different bound becomes achievable. These distinctions explain why low noise alone does not determine the attainable regret.
neurips-2024-how-does-variance-shape-the.tldr: Variance-sensitive bandit regret depends on function-class complexity, when an adversary chooses noise, and what reward information the learner receives.

paragraphs: Language models can produce harmful outputs when attackers bypass their safeguards. Refusal training teaches a model to reject requests, while adversarial training counters attacks encountered during training. This paper proposes circuit breakers, which intervene in the internal representations responsible for harmful generation as the model begins producing such responses.

The approach draws on representation engineering: controlling internal model activity to change behavior. Its target is the process leading to harmful output, giving it a different point of intervention from training responses to particular attack prompts. The authors apply the technique to both text-only and multimodal language models and report prevention of harmful generation without sacrificing utility, including under powerful attacks unseen during training.

For multimodal models, the reported protection extends to malicious images intended to steer the system into harmful responses. The paper distinguishes this system-level result from the still-open challenge of adversarial robustness in standalone image recognition. It also extends circuit breaking to agents, reporting substantial reductions in harmful actions during attacks. These findings support internal representation control as a safeguard across several kinds of model interaction.
neurips-2024-improving-alignment-and-rob.tldr: Circuit breakers intervene in internal model representations to reduce harmful outputs and agent actions, including under unseen attacks.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks encode known symmetries: transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation inside the model. These constraints can help generalization when the task has the expected structure. However, tightly enforcing them can make optimization difficult and require careful tuning. This paper asks whether temporarily relaxing the constraints can improve the training process.

The authors add a non-equivariant term to intermediate layers. This expands the set of models that training can explore to include approximately equivariant solutions. They then progressively restrict the activation magnitude of the added term, bringing the model back to an equivariant solution by the end of training. The relaxation changes the route taken through optimization while retaining equivariance as the final target.

Experiments across different state-of-the-art architectures show that this framework can improve the generalization performance of the resulting equivariant models. The finding is qualified: the method can help, rather than guaranteeing an improvement for every architecture or task. Its main idea is that a useful structural constraint need not be enforced equally strongly throughout training to benefit the final model.
neurips-2024-improving-equivariant-model.tldr: Temporarily relaxing symmetry constraints during training can produce better-generalizing models that recover equivariance at the end.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders aim to separate a language model’s internal activity into interpretable features. Evaluating whether they succeed is difficult because researchers usually lack a known collection of features that a good decomposition should recover. This paper uses models trained on board-game transcripts to create a setting where such evaluation has concrete reference points.

Chess and Othello provide naturally interpretable properties of the game state. For example, the presence of a particular piece on a particular square is a feature with a clear meaning. The authors use these collections of properties to construct metrics for sparse-autoencoder quality. This makes it possible to assess whether a learned dictionary captures meaningful state information, rather than relying only on impressions of interpretability.

The paper also introduces a sparse-autoencoder training technique called p-annealing and reports improved performance on its proposed metric. The result links a new training method to an evaluation setting with identifiable target concepts. Its contribution is both methodological and practical: board-game language models provide a concrete way to measure progress in discovering interpretable features.
neurips-2024-measuring-progress-in-dicti.tldr: Chess and Othello models provide known features for evaluating sparse autoencoders, and a new p-annealing technique improves the proposed metric.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe small input changes that would produce a favorable prediction. Those explanations also reveal information about the model itself. This paper studies how they can help train a surrogate that reproduces a target model’s predictions, particularly by exploiting their proximity to the decision boundary where predictions change.

The authors use polytope theory to derive relationships between reconstruction error and the number of counterfactual queries. This geometric analysis motivates the Counterfactual Clamping Attack. Its training loss treats counterfactual examples differently from ordinary inputs, recognizing that their location near the boundary provides information beyond their predicted class.

Treating counterfactuals as ordinary examples can shift the surrogate’s decision boundary away from the target’s. The proposed method alleviates that problem, and experiments on several datasets show improved agreement between surrogate and target predictions. The contribution connects a theoretical account of query requirements with a concrete reconstruction strategy. It also explains why an interface intended to clarify individual decisions can provide useful evidence about the broader shape of a model’s decision rule.
neurips-2024-model-reconstruction-using-.tldr: A geometry-informed training loss uses counterfactual explanations’ proximity to decision boundaries to improve model reconstruction.

paragraphs: Autoformalization translates informal mathematical material into a form that machines can verify. Training this capability requires pairs that express the same mathematical content in informal and formal language. Such data is scarce, and small manually assembled collections or few-shot prompting leave challenges in learning formal languages. This paper addresses the shortage by reversing the direction of data creation.

The authors start with formal mathematical statements and use a language model to produce corresponding informal descriptions. The resulting dataset, mma, covers multiple languages and mathematical domains. These generated pairs can then train models for the desired direction: translating informal statements into formal ones. Existing formal material thus supplies the starting point for building a larger paired dataset.

Fine-tuning on mma yields up to 29–31% of statements acceptable with minimal corrections on miniF2F and ProofNet, compared with 0% for the base model. Acceptability with corrections is the reported outcome, rather than completely correction-free formalization. The authors also find that training across multiple formal languages improves performance even on single-language tasks, supporting diversity as a useful part of autoformalization training.
neurips-2024-multi-language-diversity-be.tldr: Generating informal descriptions from formal mathematics creates useful training pairs, and formal-language diversity improves autoformalization even within one language.

paragraphs: Neural-network training often assumes that the distribution producing the data stays fixed. That assumption breaks down when supervised data shifts or when a reinforcement-learning system encounters changing learning conditions. This paper introduces a learning approach that explicitly models non-stationarity and adapts the network’s parameters as those conditions evolve.

The method links parameters through an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with an adaptive drift parameter. The drift draws parameters toward the distribution used to initialize the network. This gives the method an interpretation as a soft reset: parameters are pulled toward their initialization distribution rather than being replaced in a single reset operation. The adaptive drift makes this restoring behavior part of the learning procedure.

The authors empirically evaluate the approach in non-stationary supervised learning and off-policy reinforcement learning, reporting good performance in both settings. The contribution is a mechanism for adapting to change directly through parameter dynamics. Although the motivation includes continual learning and non-stationary contextual bandits, the stated empirical findings concern supervised and off-policy reinforcement learning.
neurips-2024-non-stationary-learning-of-.tldr: An adaptive stochastic parameter process softly pulls weights toward their initialization distribution to support learning under changing conditions.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to use experience across tasks to produce a model that adapts efficiently to a new task. This paper develops theory for that goal when training tasks are sampled independently from the same unknown task distribution. The question is how learning from those tasks supports performance on previously unseen ones with little additional data and computation.

The authors introduce uniform meta-stability, a stability notion tailored to meta-learning algorithms. They construct two algorithms satisfying this notion, using regularized empirical risk minimization and gradient descent. These constructions connect a property of the learning procedure to explicit generalization bounds, giving a theoretical basis for assessing transfer to new tasks.

The bounds cover convex learning problems with smooth losses and weakly convex problems with non-smooth losses. These specified problem classes matter to the scope of the results. The paper also extends the analysis to stochastic and adversarially robust variants of its meta-learning algorithm. Its contribution is a stability-based framework with concrete algorithmic instances and guarantees under the stated task-sampling and loss assumptions.
neurips-2024-on-the-stability-and-genera.tldr: Uniform meta-stability provides a framework for proving generalization bounds for meta-learning algorithms under specified task and loss assumptions.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a publicly available pretrained model is a common way to build a specialized system from a small dataset. This paper identifies a privacy threat in that workflow: a pretrained model can be deliberately altered so that later fine-tuning exposes more information about the victim’s training data. The authors call this a privacy backdoor.

The attack aims to strengthen black-box membership inference, which concerns determining whether data participated in training through access to the model’s behavior. Its defining feature is the timing: the attacker poisons the pretrained model before the victim uses private data for fine-tuning. The resulting model leaks membership information at a significantly higher rate than a typical fine-tuned model in the reported experiments.

The authors test the attack across datasets and model types, including CLIP vision-language models and large language models. Ablations examine different fine-tuning methods and inference strategies. These findings support the threat’s applicability across multiple evaluated workflows. The contribution is identifying how the starting checkpoint can influence the privacy leakage of a later training stage, even though the sensitive dataset enters only during that later stage.
neurips-2024-privacy-backdoors-enhancing.tldr: Poisoned pretrained checkpoints can amplify membership leakage from private data used in subsequent fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting does not always show the simple pattern that larger models and longer inputs improve predictions. More training data can help while a more capable model fails to outperform a smaller one, and a longer history can sometimes hurt. This paper proposes a scaling-law theory intended to explain these apparently inconsistent behaviors.

The framework considers dataset size, model complexity, and the granularity of the available time-series information. It gives particular attention to the look-back horizon: how much past information is supplied for forecasting. Including this input-history dimension allows the theory to address behavior that explanations based only on data quantity and model capacity leave unresolved.

The authors evaluate multiple models across diverse forecasting datasets. They report empirical support for scaling with dataset size and model complexity, as well as for the framework’s account of look-back horizon effects. The result does not imply that increasing every resource always improves a forecast. Instead, it offers a theory that accommodates the reported cases where greater capacity or longer history is unhelpful, with potential relevance to both limited-data forecasting and larger foundational models.
neurips-2024-scaling-law-for-time-series.tldr: A forecasting scaling theory incorporates input-history length to explain why more data, larger models, and longer contexts do not help uniformly.

paragraphs: Visual representation learning often teaches models to ignore image transformations such as crops or color changes. That helps recognize shared content, but it can discard information needed for precise localization or fine-grained classification. Equivariant learning instead retains information about how an image changes. Existing methods often require transformation labels, making complex or interdependent changes difficult to handle.

Self-supervised Transformation Learning replaces those labels with transformation representations learned from image pairs. The method makes the representation of a transformation independent of the particular image and learns corresponding changes in the image representation. This lets the model capture transformation-sensitive information without increasing batch complexity or requiring an explicit label for each transformation.

The authors report better results than existing methods on 7 of 11 classification and detection benchmarks, with particularly strong detection performance. They also incorporate complex transformations such as AugMix that prior equivariant methods could not use, improving performance across tasks. Compatibility with multiple base models supports the method’s flexibility. The central contribution is learning how transformations should be represented, expanding the transformations that equivariant representation learning can accommodate.
neurips-2024-self-supervised-transformat.tldr: STL learns transformation representations from image pairs, enabling equivariant learning with complex augmentations and improving several classification and detection benchmarks.

paragraphs: Selecting useful supervised fine-tuning data can reduce training costs, but specialized examples differ in how they influence learning. SmallToLarge uses a small reference model to study that behavior. It records how each example’s loss changes during training, groups examples with similar loss trajectories, and samples from those groups to select data for a larger model.

The theoretical argument connects similar loss trajectories to similar gradients during fine-tuning. The authors show that the selected subset has bounded gradient error relative to the full dataset, supporting convergence to a neighborhood of the optimum. This gives trajectory clustering a learning-based justification beyond grouping examples by their content.

On mathematical problem-solving, S2L matches full-data performance using 11% of MathInstruct and outperforms leading selection methods by an average of 4.7% across six evaluations. Using 50,000 examples, it reaches 32.7% accuracy on MATH. On MIMIC-III clinical summarization, half the data outperforms full-data training. The method also supports a reference model 100 times smaller than the target, reducing the computation needed for selection. These findings demonstrate data savings in the evaluated domains.
neurips-2024-smalltolarge-s2l-scalable-d.tldr: S2L selects fine-tuning examples by clustering their learning trajectories in a small model, achieving strong results with substantially less data.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents usually act before observing the rewards their actions produce. In some settings, however, useful reward information arrives beforehand, such as transaction prices or a goal provided before interaction. This paper asks how much that advance information can improve achievable reward, rather than treating all agents as having the same information when they act.

The authors use competitive analysis to compare the value of a standard agent with that of an agent receiving partial information about future rewards. They characterize worst-case reward distributions and derive exact ratios between the corresponding expected rewards. This supplies a quantitative measure of the advantage associated with lookahead under the analyzed worst-case conditions.

The results cover a range of information access, from seeing immediate rewards before choosing an action to seeing all rewards before interaction begins. The paper also derives tight ratio bounds under worst-case environment dynamics. Connections to quantities from offline reinforcement learning and reward-free exploration emerge from the analysis. The contribution is a theoretical account of how the timing and extent of reward information change what an agent can achieve.
neurips-2024-the-value-of-reward-lookahe.tldr: The paper derives worst-case reward ratios quantifying the advantage of observing some or all future rewards before acting.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how the amount of next-token training data affects learning hierarchical language structure. It begins with synthetic sequences generated by a probabilistic context-free grammar, which creates tree-like relationships. This controlled setting lets the authors analytically calculate correlations between tokens and connect observable patterns to the grammar’s hidden variables.

Longer-range correlations can reveal variables deeper in the hierarchy. A finite dataset, however, only resolves correlations over an effective range, and that range increases with dataset size. The resulting explanation is that more examples can enable a language model to represent deeper grammatical structure. It links the benefit of additional data to which structural relationships become statistically detectable.

The authors conjecture that the relationship between dataset size and effective correlation range extends beyond their synthetic setting, and test it on lines from Shakespeare’s plays. They show that shortening the input causes improvements in test loss to saturate at a characteristic dataset size predicted by the framework. The broader extension remains a conjecture, while the experiments support the proposed connection between available context, data quantity, and learnable structure.
neurips-2024-towards-a-theory-of-how-the.tldr: A grammar-based theory links more training data to detectable longer-range correlations and deeper representations of language structure.

paragraphs: Analog energy-based circuits offer an alternative route to neural-network training, but practical accelerators also rely on digital computation. This combination needs a training framework that connects the two kinds of components. The paper introduces feedforward-tied energy-based models, which combine digital feedforward blocks with analog energy-based blocks.

The authors derive an end-to-end gradient algorithm that uses backpropagation through feedforward components and Equilibrium Propagation through energy-based components. This allows the two training mechanisms to operate within one model. The approach gives Equilibrium Propagation a role in mixed architectures, supporting gradual integration of analog computational blocks into existing digital systems.

Experiments use Deep Hopfield Networks as the energy-based blocks. The authors show that a standard network can be divided into blocks of any uniform size while maintaining or improving performance, with simulation speedups reaching fourfold. On ImageNet32, the hybrid models achieve 46% top-1 performance, reported as a new best result in the Equilibrium Propagation literature. The speed finding concerns simulation; the broader contribution is a principled gradient framework for training hybrid digital and analog architectures.
neurips-2024-towards-training-digitally-.tldr: A hybrid gradient algorithm connects backpropagation and Equilibrium Propagation to train models combining digital feedforward and analog energy-based blocks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks a good policy from previously collected experience. This paper assumes every policy’s action-value function is linear in a given feature representation, along with a coverage condition limiting how far policies’ state-action distributions can depart from the dataset distribution. Earlier negative results using individual transitions left open whether complete trajectories could make efficient learning possible.

The authors prove that trajectories do make a difference. A sufficient dataset size is polynomial in feature dimension, horizon, and the coverage coefficient, multiplied by the inverse square of the desired accuracy. Crucially, this requirement does not depend on the number of states. The result establishes statistical efficiency under the specified representation and coverage assumptions.

The proof uses an approximation of the assumed environment by a linear Markov decision process. That approximation involves skipping certain states, creating estimation problems that are straightforward with complete trajectories but remain difficult with separate transitions. Thus, the sequence structure of the data is central to the result. Whether learning can also be computationally efficient under these assumptions remains open.
neurips-2024-trajectory-data-suffices-fo.tldr: Under linear value-function and coverage assumptions, full trajectories enable offline learning with sample requirements independent of state-space size.

paragraphs: Prior-data fitted networks use pretraining and in-context learning to classify new tabular data in a single forward pass. Their appeal is strong performance without training a new model from scratch for every task. However, TabPFN was designed for small datasets and does not support prediction for datasets larger than 1,000 examples in its original form.

TuneTables addresses this constraint by learning a smaller context that compresses information from a larger dataset. Its parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy optimizes this context, providing a way to adapt a pretrained network while keeping the amount of adjusted model capacity small. The central idea is that the model’s context can become a learned representation of the task’s data.

Across 19 algorithms and 98 datasets, TuneTables achieves the strongest average performance, including outperforming CatBoost, while optimizing fewer than 5% of TabPFN’s parameters. An average result does not imply winning on every dataset. The authors also show uses for interpretability and bias mitigation through a fairness objective. Context optimization therefore serves both as a scaling mechanism and as a way to shape task-specific behavior.
neurips-2024-tunetables-context-optimiza.tldr: TuneTables compresses large tabular datasets into a learned context, extending TabPFN’s scale and improving average benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Some transformer neurons develop activations much larger than those of other neurons. These outlier features make quantization harder, complicating the use of lower-precision representations. The paper investigates how they arise during training and how architectural and optimization choices can reduce them before quantization takes place.

The authors first establish quantitative measures of outliers, including kurtosis over neuron activation norms. They use these measures to study training choices and introduce an unnormalized transformer component called the Outlier Protected block. They also identify a benefit of non-diagonal preconditioning optimizers. Both approaches substantially reduce outlier features and improve quantization without compromising convergence speed in experiments reaching seven billion parameters.

For OPT-125m, combining the Outlier Protected block with SOAP yields perplexity of 14.87 after eight-bit weight-and-activation quantization, compared with 14.71 at standard precision. A Pre-Norm model trained with Adam changes from 16.00 to 63.4 under the reported quantization comparison. This example illustrates how training choices can preserve model quality when precision is reduced. The contribution connects measurable activation behavior to practical architecture and optimizer changes.
neurips-2024-understanding-and-minimisin.tldr: An Outlier Protected transformer block and non-diagonal preconditioning reduce oversized activations and improve quantization while preserving convergence speed.
